title: How Much Should You Save If You’re Self-Employed With Irregular Income
description: Calculating your 'Freedom Number' when you don't have a salary.
content:
Self-employment offers unlimited upside but zero safety net. When you are the boss, a slow month doesn't just mean no bonus; it means no rent money. Therefore, the savings requirements for freelancers are significantly higher than for employees. You aren't just saving for a rainy day; you are saving for 'Business Continuity,' 'Taxes,' and 'Benefits.' This guide helps you calculate the specific cash targets needed to sleep well at night while riding the revenue rollercoaster.

Key Takeaways

  • The 3-Bucket System: You need Personal Savings (6 months), Business Operating Savings (3 months), and Tax Savings (30% of revenue). Mixing these is fatal.
  • The Tax Trap: The most common reason freelancers fail is spending their tax money. You must save ~30% of every check immediately. The IRS is your silent partner.
  • Retirement Catch-Up: Without an employer match, you must save 20% of your net income to stay on par with corporate peers. Use a Solo 401(k).
  • Variable Budgeting: Your savings rate should float. In a $10k month, save $5k. In a $4k month, save $0. Don't force a flat rate.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US 'Self-Employment Tax' (15.3%) is on top of Income Tax. This means $100 of freelance income is really only ~$70 of spendable cash. Adjust your mental math to see $100 as $70 instantly.

The Savings Hierarchy

Prioritize your cash flow in this order.

Priority 1: The Tax Vault (30%)

Goal: $0 balance on April 15.

Action: Every time a client pays, move 30% to a separate HYSA. Pay quarterly estimates. Never touch this.

Priority 2: The 'Famine' Fund (Personal)

Goal: 6-9 months of personal expenses.

Why high? If you lose a major client, it takes 3-6 months to replace that revenue pipeline. You need a longer runway than a W-2 worker.

Priority 3: The 'OpEx' Fund (Business)

Goal: 2 months of business overhead (Software, Contractors).

Why: You don't want to fire your assistant or cancel your website hosting just because a client paid late.

How to Save 20% for Retirement

  1. Open a Solo 401(k): This allows you to contribute $23,000 (Employee) + 20% of Profit (Employer). It drastically lowers your taxable income.
  2. The 'Sweep' Method: Pick a 'Cap' for your checking account (e.g., $5,000). On the last day of the month, sweep anything above $5,000 into the Solo 401(k).
  3. Invest the Tax Fund: Keep your tax money in a T-Bill ladder or Money Market Fund earning 5%. You hold the cash for months before paying the IRS; might as well earn interest on it.
  4. The 'Profit First' Mindset: Take your profit (savings) off the top, not the bottom. If you can't run the business on the remainder, your expenses are too high.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if I have a bad month?

Stop saving. Live on the 'Base Salary' you pay yourself from the business account. If the business account is empty, dip into the Famine Fund. That is its job.

Can I use my emergency fund to buy equipment?

No. That is a capital expense. Save for a new laptop in a separate 'Sinking Fund'. Emergency funds are for survival, not growth.

Do I need disability insurance?

Yes. If you break your hand and can't type/work, your income stops. You have no sick leave. Own-Occupation Disability Insurance is mandatory for freelancers.
